objective.statement: Transpose a short melody between concert pitch and the written part for an instrument in B♭, A or F, with the right key signature and accidentals.
successCriteria: I find the new key before moving the notes.
I move every note by the same interval, adjusting accidentals by the interval.
I do not respell a note as its enharmonic equivalent.

explanation.text: To transpose a melody for one of these instruments, first find the new key. The question tells you which interval to use and whether to go up or down. A melody in D major, to be written for a clarinet in A (up a minor 3rd), becomes F major: D up a minor 3rd is F. Then write the new key signature, and then every note.

music.textAlternative: A four-note phrase in D major at concert pitch: D, F sharp, A, F sharp.

explanation.caption: At concert pitch, in D major.

music.textAlternative: The same phrase written for a clarinet in A, in F major: F, A, C, A.

explanation.caption: Written for a clarinet in A, up a minor 3rd: F major.

explanation.text: Do not assume the accidentals stay the same. Every note moves by the same interval, so each note keeps its relation to the tonic. A G♯ in D major is an augmented 4th above the tonic; an augmented 4th above F is B natural, so the G♯ becomes B♮ in F major (not B♭).

Do not respell a note as its enharmonic twin. B natural could be written C♭ and would sound the same, but C♭ is a diminished 5th above F, not an augmented 4th, so it would be wrong. Always move the letter names by the interval. Copy over any performance directions (tempo, dynamics, slurs) that the original has, as you would for a real performance. You may also be asked to check someone else's transposition: find the new key first and compare the key signature, then check each note against the interval, one at a time.
New key first, then the key signature, then every note by the same interval. Concert to written goes up; written to concert goes down.

music.textAlternative: A phrase in A minor at concert pitch.

steps: Concert pitch to the written part for a clarinet in B♭: up a tone.
A minor up a tone is B minor.
Move every note up a tone: B D F♯ D.
demonstration.textAlternative: A minor phrase moved up a tone to B minor.

guided.prompt: The written part for a cor anglais (in F) is in A minor. In which key does it sound (concert pitch)?

E minor.reason: That moves the key the wrong way: the sound is lower than the written part.

F minor.reason: F minor is the name of the instrument, not the key of the music: transpose the key by the instrument's interval.

A minor.reason: That is the key of the music you were given: a transposed part needs a different key signature.

hints: Move the key by the instrument's interval, in the right direction.
Move the key down a perfect 5th, as you would move any note.

mistakes.wrong-clef: Look at which clef the question asks for — alto and tenor clefs are easy to mix up.
mistakes.wrong-interval: B♭ is a tone, A a minor 3rd and F a perfect 5th.
mistakes.wrong-direction: Written pitch is higher than concert pitch for these instruments.
mistakes.key-signature-missing: A transposed part needs the key signature of its new key.
mistakes.accidental-not-adjusted: Accidentals change too. Work out what each altered note is in the original key, then find the same degree in the new key.
mistakes.enharmonic-respelling: Move every letter by the same number of steps.
